planting.note: Divide rhizomes or set transplants into pure long-fiber sphagnum or a 1:1 peat-perlite mix, never fertilized potting soil, and stand the pot in a tray of rain or distilled water year-round.

directions: This warm-climate counterpart to the northern purple pitcher plant forms a low rosette of squat, heavily flared pitchers with a fuzzy inner throat that traps ants and other crawling insects rather than relying on rainfall drowning alone. It thrives across the southeastern coastal plain in open, sunny bogs and tolerates summer heat far better than the straight species, though it still needs a distinct cooler winter rest with reduced watering. Keep roots constantly wet with pure water in a peat-based mix and give it as much direct sun as possible for the best pitcher color and reddish venation. It hybridizes readily with other Sarracenia species, and many garden-grown clumps are actually venosa crosses rather than pure forms.

planting.note: Divide bulb-like rhizomes and pot into pure sphagnum moss or a 1:1 peat-perlite mix, keeping the tray sitting in rain or distilled water; propagate true-to-type by division since seed-grown offspring do not reliably inherit the fused teeth.

directions: This distinctive flytrap cultivar is prized for its cilia, which fuse together into a jagged, saw-like ridge along each trap lobe instead of forming the usual widely spaced spikes seen on typical Venus flytraps. Grow it exactly as you would a standard flytrap, in pure nutrient-free sphagnum or peat-perlite media kept constantly moist with rain or distilled water, with full sun for the reddest trap coloration. It needs a cool, several-month winter dormancy with reduced light and near-freezing root temperatures to stay vigorous long-term, just like the species. Because the fused-tooth trait can segregate out in seedlings, growers maintain this clone by dividing rhizome offshoots rather than growing from seed.

planting.note: Divide rhizomes and pot into pure sphagnum moss or a 1:1 peat-perlite mix; grow under strong light so the traps color up fully red rather than staying green.

directions: This vigorous flytrap cultivar develops traps that flush a deep, even red both inside and out even under moderate light, unlike many red-trap selections that need intense sun to color up. It is otherwise cared for like any Venus flytrap, potted in pure nutrient-free sphagnum or a peat-perlite blend and kept standing in a tray of rain or distilled water at all times. Provide a cool winter dormancy of several months with reduced light so the rhizome can rest and rebuild vigor for the following growing season. Divide established clumps every couple of years to keep the planting from overcrowding and to propagate more true-to-type plants.

planting.note: Surface-sow dust-like seed onto pure milled sphagnum or a 1:1 peat-sand mix and keep constantly wet in a humidity dome; move outdoors to a bog tray only after temperatures stay reliably above 65F.

directions: This compact rosette sundew is one of the fastest-growing carnivorous plants available to hobbyists, reaching flowering size from seed in just a couple of months and readily self-sowing in a bog tray. Its short, sticky-glanded leaves fold inward within minutes of catching gnats or fruit flies, among the quickest leaf movement of any Drosera. Give it full sun, constant standing water, and a warm, humid growing spot, since it has no cold-hardy dormancy and is treated as a warm-season annual outside the tropics. It thrives in containers on a sunny patio all summer but should be brought indoors to a terrarium or grow light before the first frost.

planting.note: Press small pieces of rhizome or existing sod onto the surface of a wet peat-sand mix or pure milled sphagnum; keep constantly saturated to boggy in a shallow tray and never let it dry out.

directions: This small South African terrestrial bladderwort forms a dense green mat that stays inconspicuous until it blooms, sending up thin stalks of pale lilac to white flowers whose two upper petal lobes flare out like a pair of rabbit ears. It captures microscopic soil organisms with tiny underground bladder traps rather than visible leaf structures, so all the interest is in the near-constant flowering rather than dramatic foliage. Grow it in shallow trays of wet peat-based mix under bright indirect light or fluorescent grow lights, and it will spread quickly by rhizome to fill a pot within a season. It is frost-tender and best kept as a windowsill, terrarium, or greenhouse subject outside zones 9 to 11.

planting.note: Press rhizome fragments or sod pieces onto the surface of a wet peat-sand or peat-perlite mix and keep the tray flooded shallowly; it tolerates lower humidity and light better than most terrestrial bladderworts.

directions: Native to southern and eastern Africa, this easygoing terrestrial bladderwort is often recommended as a beginner's introduction to the genus because it tolerates a wider range of light and moisture than most Utricularia species. It forms a low mat of thread-like stems studded with microscopic underground bladders that suck in and digest tiny soil-dwelling protozoa and nematodes, and it flowers nearly year-round with small white-to-pale-violet blooms marked by a yellow-green throat spot. Keep it in a shallow tray of wet peat-based mix that never dries out, with bright indirect light or a windowsill spot. It spreads readily and can be divided at almost any time to start new pots or share with other growers.

planting.note: Set divisions or seed-grown plugs into a lean, mineral mix such as 1:1 peat and sand or coarse perlite, and keep constantly moist; unlike Mexican butterworts it needs a true winter with cold, wet dormancy and forms a tight, protective hibernaculum bud when temperatures drop.

directions: Unlike the succulent-leaved Mexican butterworts more commonly seen in cultivation, this circumboreal species is a true cold-climate bog plant found across northern Europe, Asia, and North America in wet, mossy fens and lake margins. Its sticky, pale yellow-green leaves lie flat in a rosette and lure and digest small flying insects through the same glue-trap mechanism as its relatives, while a single violet flower rises on a thin stalk each spring. It requires an actual freezing winter to survive, dying back to a tight bud-like hibernaculum that resists ice and resumes growth the following spring, so it fails in warm climates without a cold dormancy period. Grow it in a lean, constantly wet peat-sand mix in a bog garden or unheated cold frame, and avoid the summer bright-sun exposure that Mexican Pinguicula species tolerate.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings or pot on nursery starts in a well-draining, nutrient-free mix of long-fiber sphagnum, perlite, and orchid bark; grow in a warm, humid spot with bright indirect light and never let the roots sit in fertilized soil.

directions: The most widespread Nepenthes species in the wild, ranging from southern China through Southeast Asia to northern Australia, this vining tropical pitcher plant is also one of the easiest for beginners because it tolerates a broader range of temperature, humidity, and light than most of its highland relatives. It produces slender green to reddish pitchers that hang from tendril tips at the end of each leaf, filling with digestive fluid that drowns and breaks down insects for nutrients in nutrient-poor peat swamps and disturbed ground. Because it is a lowland species, it grows best with warm days and nights that don't drop much below 65F, unlike cooler-growing highland Nepenthes, and it appreciates high humidity, bright filtered light, and constant moisture from rainwater or distilled water. Its adaptability and vigor have made it a parent of countless popular hybrids sold to home growers, so acquiring the true species offers a useful comparison plant for a home pitcher plant collection.
